When temperatures get to 40C inside, and French building regulations won’t even allow shutters, these tenants’ listed homes are simply unlivable
The population of Firminy, south-east France, has been dwindling for decades. Its recent history is one of factory closures in a region built by steel, and locals tell me that many people leave for better opportunities in neighbouring Saint-Étienne, or to live in the Haute-Loire’s countryside.
On the top of a hill, however, stands Firminy’s pride: l’Unité d’Habitation, an imposing tower of concrete designed by Le Corbusier. The architect’s final project is an oddity – a building for people, where two-thirds of the apartments are dedicated to habitations à loyer modéré (or HLM – social housing); but also a piece of history, whose facade and roof were listed as monuments historiquesin 1993.
It was also designed for a 1960s climate, not the sweltering temperatures we have experienced for much of the summer. For its residents, the tower feels increasingly like an unlivable furnace – and because of its protected status, that is unlikely to change soon.
We are on the brink of the fourth heatwave of the year when I meet a group of residents at the bottom of l’Unité d’Habitation. They have had enough. Inside their flats, during a heatwave, the temperatures regularly reach 35C, and can rise to 40C.
“I slept on the floor because it was the only place I could stay cool,” says Aurélie Mohamed, who has lived in l’Unité d’Habitation for five years.
“I slept on the balcony,” says Nathalie Rouchouse, who moved in 15 years ago.
“My godmother was one of the original residents of Le Corbusier, and I can remember coming here aged nine,” Chantal Hospital tells me. “We marvelled at the building; we were so proud of it in Firminy. It’s been 26 years since I moved in, and now I’m doing my best to move out. I never want to live in a historic monument again.”
L’Unité d’Habitation has no shutters, but adding them would not be a straightforward task. Any change to the facade of a historic monument is subject to a long list of rules, and can’t currently be done without the authorisation of the architectes des bâtiments de France (ABF). For now, residents resort to DIY methods, hanging blankets or panels made from tinfoil across the windows, but it’s no substitute.
When a person owns a part of a historic monument, as is the case with the third of apartments in private ownership in l’Unité d’Habitation in Firminy, there are certain benefits to its listed status. They are entitled to a grant of 40% of the cost of the work when they carry out renovations, and they are able to claim some tax reductions.
But social renters are caught in the middle of the rules imposed on all historic monuments in the country, and the actions and investment of Habitat et Métropole, the social landlord that manages the HLM part of the building. Habitat et Métropole didn’t answer any of my questions regarding the Firminy site.
The relentless heatwaves have highlighted a class divide in France. The residents of l’Unité d’Habitation are far from the only ones living in HLMs to complain of 40C inside their homes, and in some respects they are better off than those in poorly designed buildings elsewhere. Le Corbusier’s famous pilotis allow for better airflow underneath the tower.
This class element is even more apparent in Firminy, where the Le Corbusier site, including parts of l’Unité d’Habitation, is also a tourist attraction. About 20,000 visitors a year come to see l’Unité d’Habitation, its showroom apartment and the kindergarten, which is no longer used as a nursery. Aurélie Mohamed, Nathalie Rouchouse and Chantal Hospital’s home is a living museum, but although tourists pay to visit their building, none of the money from ticket sales is injected back into the site. It is run as a separate operation and Géraldine Dabrigeon, the chief curator of Site Le Corbusier, says that the revenue from ticket sales only covers guides, advertising and insurance. Even though the part open to tourists is run separately, it strikes me as rather zoo-like to have people paying to visit somewhere while the residents swelter behind blankets hung to compensate for the lack of shutters.
Le Corbusier’s vertical towns were built at a time when social initiatives were booming, and they were designed to support those on lower incomes. Now, the very people these buildings are designed for are being penalised for living in a keepsake of France’s social history.
Under a new proposal, brought forward by the French government on 7 July in response to the heatwaves, local councils could gain greater power to modify historic buildings. Rather than the ABF having the definitive say on any modifications, its opinion would be regarded as merely advisory. Critics in the conservative newspaper Le Figaro say that such a move would lead to a “concrete and soulless France”. But the residents of l’Unité d’Habitation already live in a concrete block – one without shutters.
“At some point, a choice will need to be made,” says Chantal Hospital. “Does the building stay residential, as Corbusier intended, or does it become a museum?”
The problem isn’t necessarily that l’Unité d’Habitation is a historic monument, but rather that HLMs across France leave the poorest and most vulnerable suffering the worst of the heatwaves. To be both a historic monument and an HLM, however, means to have all the disadvantages of an underfunded HLM while also being subject to the list of strict rules imposed on historic monuments. It makes the prestige of their “monument historique” plaque rather hollow for the renters – especially when their makeshift provisions for the heat can be gawked at by visiting tourists. At what point do we respect architecture and history over people’s living conditions?
Speaking under the tower, residents told me they had been raising these issues for years. But the Fondation Le Corbusier only discussed the increasing impact of heatwaves on the various Le Corbusier sites this year, one board member said. It plans to look through his old architectural plans to see if it would be possible to install shutters that fit with the listed facade. If the foundation fights sufficiently for its residents, particularly those in HLMs, perhaps the renters will finally reap the rewards of living in a listed building. The fact that this is only just being discussed, however, makes me feel this may be too little, too late.
There is also a significant risk that the HLM renters of l’Unité d’Habitation will fall foul of the famous complexities of French bureaucracy, in a case of too many cooks. In that instance, the whole complex affair could drag on for so long that these homes become uninhabitable.
The number of heatwaves is expected to increase fivefold in France by 2050. While the rich are largely responsible for the climate crisis, those living in social housing, without air conditioning or shutters, will be the first to suffer the consequences.
Anna Richards is a journalist and travel writer based in Lyon

Scramble to house hundreds camping in Rome heatwave after squat eviction
Officials try to find homes for residents as talks to save social assistance hub collapse amid government crackdown
Rome authorities are scrambling to find homes for hundreds of people sleeping in tents in extreme heat after talks aimed at saving Italy’s most high-profile centre for housing and social assistance collapsed amid a crackdown by Giorgia Meloni’s government on squatted buildings.
The approximately 400 evicted residents of Spin Time Labs, located in a 10-floor building in Rome’s Esquilino district occupied by grassroots groups since 2013, will not be allowed to move back in after its private owner refused Rome council’s offer to buy the property. The residents were forced out at the end of last month.
A spokesperson for Italy’s interior ministry, which had set its sights on shutting down Spin Time, confirmed that the owner had taken repossession of the building “in accordance with the law”.
The move has reignited political debate over occupied or squatted buildings, which Meloni’s government regard as dens for criminality – including those supported by leftwing associations. Critics have questioned why Meloni and her coalition allies have long been so decisively against Spin Time while the neofascist CasaPound has occupied a state-owned building in the same neighbourhood for more than 20 years, using the premises as its headquarters.
People of all nationalities, about a quarter of them children, were forced to evacuate Spin Time on 29 July after a minor fire, which was quickly extinguished by a group of residents before it could spread.
The building was locked up by police during safety checks, before being placed under two judicial seizure orders – one linked to the owner’s long-running legal battle to regain possession and the other to the fire.
While some people were accommodated by friends and family, more than 200, including elderly people and those with ill health, have been sleeping in tents outside the building. One child was hospitalised this week after suffering breathing difficulties.
Rome’s leftwing council, supported by the Catholic church-run charity Caritas, is now seeking alternative solutions.
In an interview on In Onda, a talkshow broadcast on the TV channel LA7, the mayor of Rome, Roberto Gualtieri, said the response to the council’s offer had been an “irrevocable no” and that despite presenting what he believed was the best possible deal he “had the impression that the decision had already been taken”.
The owner had cited unspecified legal weaknesses in the proposal, Gualtieri said, adding that he felt “irritated” about the situation.
He described Spin Time, which over the past decade has transformed into a space offering various social and cultural services, including a food bank, a restaurant and co-working, as “the mirror of a failure of Italy’s Second Republic, which stripped away a pillar of welfare”. The Second Republic is a political term for the era of government that began in the early 1990s.
The initiative has provided a lifeline for hundreds of people, including Marco Perilli, an Italian construction worker who was one of the community’s first residents. He became homeless after a divorce.
As of Friday, people were still camped outside. Perilli said they would continue to do so until a real solution was found. “We are trying to understand how things will proceed but we resist and will continue to resist. The owner refusing the offer means Spin Time is over, but for us it’s not over – we will find another space.”

Slurred Speech in the Heat? Why You Should Call 119 Immediately
■Yoo Moon-young, Professor of Family Medicine, Hallym University Dongtan Sacred Heart Hospital
Prevent heat-related illness by avoiding midday outdoor activity and staying hydrated
When using air conditioning for long periods, indoor ventilation and filter maintenance are essential
Food poisoning risk also surges; seek immediate care if urine output drops
Even with low blood pressure and dizziness, never stop prescribed medication on your own
Culture||
By Ahn Kyung-jin, Medical Correspondent
||
As record-breaking heat waves continue, not only outdoor activities but daily life itself is placing a burden on health. When temperature and humidity rise, regulating body temperature becomes difficult, and heavy sweating drains water and electrolytes, increasing the risk of dehydration and heat-related illness. Food spoils easily, raising the risk of food poisoning, while skin damage from strong ultraviolet rays is also common. In particular, the elderly, infants and toddlers, and patients with chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease require special caution, as even mild dehydration or a rise in body temperature can cause their condition to deteriorate rapidly.
The first situations to guard against during a heat wave are heat-related illnesses such as heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Heat exhaustion, commonly described as being "overcome by the heat," occurs when heavy sweating leaves water and salt inadequately replenished. Symptoms can include dizziness, weakness, headache, nausea, and muscle cramps. When heat exhaustion is suspected, move to a cool place immediately, loosen clothing, and rest while sipping small amounts of water or electrolyte drinks.
By contrast, if body temperature rises sharply and consciousness becomes clouded, or if speech and behavior differ from usual and symptoms such as convulsions or fainting appear, heat stroke should be suspected. Heat stroke usually involves body temperature rising to 40 degrees or higher accompanied by changes in consciousness. It is an emergency condition that can be fatal if not treated promptly, so call 119 immediately and lower the body temperature using wet towels or cold water until the ambulance arrives. However, do not force water or drinks on someone whose consciousness is not clear.
On days when a heat wave warning has been issued, avoid outdoor activity during the hottest part of the day. If going out is unavoidable, it is advisable to wear breathable, light-colored clothing and a hat. Alcohol worsens dehydration, so heavy drinking should be avoided.
The foundation of summer health management is adequate hydration. A significant number of patients who visit the hospital for urinary stones have neglected hydration in their daily lives. If water lost through sweat is not replenished in time, dehydration can cause dizziness and lethargy. As urine becomes concentrated, the risk of urinary stones also increases. Rather than drinking a large amount of water all at once after feeling thirsty, it is better to drink small amounts frequently as a habit. The best beverage is water. If you have sweated heavily from prolonged outdoor activity, sports drinks can help replenish electrolytes, but continuously drinking high-sugar beverages in place of water is not advisable. However, patients whose water intake is restricted due to heart failure or chronic kidney disease should not drink large amounts of water indiscriminately. It is important to follow the water intake amount advised by medical staff while monitoring for changes such as weight gain, edema, or difficulty breathing. Using air conditioning for long periods can cause so-called "air conditioning sickness" symptoms such as headache, fatigue, muscle pain, nasal congestion, and indigestion due to the temperature difference between indoors and outdoors. Do not set the indoor temperature too low, and prevent cold air from directly hitting the body. Preparing a thin outer garment and ventilating the room every one to two hours is also helpful. Air conditioner filters should be cleaned periodically to prevent the buildup of dust and microorganisms. If cough, high fever, and difficulty breathing accompany the symptoms, do not simply dismiss them as air conditioning sickness, but seek medical care to rule out other conditions such as respiratory infection. Strong ultraviolet rays in summer cause sunburn and skin aging, and over the long term can raise the risk of skin cancer and eye disease. When going out, apply plenty of sunscreen and make active use of hats, sunglasses, parasols, and long-sleeved clothing.
In hot and humid weather, bacteria multiply easily, creating a high risk of food poisoning. Wash your hands frequently, cook food thoroughly all the way through, and keep separate knives and cutting boards for raw meat and vegetables. Do not leave cooked food at room temperature for long periods; refrigerate it promptly, and it is safest not to eat food whose storage condition is in doubt. When symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and vomiting appear, replenish fluids in small amounts frequently, but seek medical care if accompanied by bloody stool, high fever, severe abdominal pain, decreased urine output, or diminished consciousness.
In summer, blood pressure can be lower than usual as blood vessels dilate and dehydration compounds the effect. You should not stop or reduce blood pressure medication or diuretics on your own just because you feel dizzy. The first priority is to determine whether the drop in blood pressure is caused by dehydration, medication dosage, or another condition. If dizziness or lethargy persists, or if blood pressure is repeatedly measured low, consult your attending medical staff. If you have elderly relatives living alone or family members with limited mobility, check on them frequently. Simply checking whether the indoor space is too hot, whether they are eating well, and whether they seem unusually weak or drowsy can prevent serious accidents.
There is no special secret to summer health management. The basics are to stay well hydrated, avoid overexertion, and maintain regular meals and sleep. By not missing the warning signals your body sends and following preventive guidelines, you can enjoy a safer and healthier summer.

Commuters wade through heavy rainfall near Connaught Place, in New Delhi on Friday. Photograph: (ANI)
Story highlights
Delhi recorded its wettest first week of August since 2011 with 127 mm of rain. Heavy showers caused waterlogging and traffic disruptions, while the IMD issued a yellow alert and forecast more rain till Aug 10.
Delhi witnessed its wettest first week of August since 2011 after incessant rains resulted in waterlogging in several parts of the city, disrupting traffic movement. While continuous showers during the day brought relief from the heat, they caused inconvenience to commuters. The national capital received 127 mm of rainfall in the first seven days of the month. On Friday (Aug 7), several weather stations in the city recorded more than 100 mm of rain.
Delhi typically receives around 42 mm of rainfall during the first week of August, based on data from the past two decades. This year, however, rainfall in the opening seven days of the month surged to 127 mm after Friday’s downpour. Meanwhile, the driest first week of August since 2011 was recorded in 2015, when the city received just 3 mm of rain.
South Delhi’s Pushp Vihar recorded the highest rainfall during the day at 111.5 mm, followed by Chhatarpur with 104.5 mm. Other areas that received substantial rainfall included Ayanagar (87.4 mm), Palam (73.5 mm), Janakpuri (68 mm), Jharoda Kalan (67 mm), Pusa (59.5 mm), Safdarjung (57.3 mm), Narayana (53 mm), Ridge (49.6 mm), Lodhi Road (49.3 mm), Mayur Vihar (36 mm), Najafgarh (24 mm), and Jafarpur (13.5 mm).
Persistent rainfall throughout the day narrowed the gap between the maximum and minimum temperatures to just 1.9 degrees Celsius. The maximum temperature settled at 27.5 degrees Celsius, seven degrees below normal and nearly unchanged from Thursday’s 27.6 degrees Celsius. The minimum temperature was 25.6 degrees Celsius, one degree below normal and the same as the previous day.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has predicted more rain on Saturday (Aug 8) and issued a yellow alert. The wet spell is likely to remain till August 10.
